asDecan.p: Each sign gets cut into three ten-degree slices called decans, each with a planet of its own. Your Sun sits between ten and nineteen degrees of Aquarius, the middle third, where the sign is at full strength, and the Golden Dawn gives that stretch to Mercury, the planet of thinking and talking. In Aquarius it has no special dignity, which just means it's a visitor there, neither helped nor held back. Aquarius is ruled by Saturn in the old system and Uranus in the modern one, so your Mercury gets Saturn's patience and Uranus's knack for looking at things from somewhere odd. The Five of Swords before you belongs to Venus and is about who won the argument. The Seven after you is the Moon's, and it slips off quietly with what it wants. Yours is the boat in the middle, being poled across to calmer water. The Star is still your Sun card, and this is the finer grain inside it.

When a friend rings in a state, you're the one who talks them down, usually by asking practical questions until the panic has nowhere left to go. In a meeting that's turned into two people shouting, you're the one who says, fairly mildly, can we write down what we actually agree on. You move house more than most people, or at least you think about it more, and there's a folder somewhere of places you might live one day. When a group chat blows up you tend to read the lot, say nothing for a day, and then send one long, careful message that sorts it out. On a Sunday with nothing planned you'll often go for a long drive or a train ride just to think. Movement helps your head, and you've probably known that since you were a kid.

The second gift is that you're good at getting other people out of things. When a friend finally decides to leave a bad marriage or a job that's grinding them down, you're the one who turns up with boxes, finds the rental listings, and knows what to say to the landlord. You don't make them talk about their feelings before they're ready. You just get them moving, and the talking happens on the way, which is often when people can actually manage it. I've seen this a lot with Suns in this part of Aquarius. They end up as the unofficial ferryman in the family, the one a sister rings at eleven at night saying she's in the car and doesn't know where to go. And you're calm on those calls in a way that settles the other person too.

The less obvious trouble is that you can think you've dealt with something because you've understood it. You can explain exactly why the relationship ended, what each of you did and how it fits a pattern, and still not have cried about it once. The swords are still in the boat. Then there's the way you leave. You tend to decide in private, sometimes over months, and announce it once it's settled, so the other person gets the news and the finished plan at the same time. A flatmate finds out you're moving from a note on the fridge. A partner hears that you've been unhappy since the spring. From your side it was a long and careful process. From theirs it came out of nowhere, and that can sting worse than the leaving itself.

When something goes badly wrong, a death in the family or a job falling through, the first thing you do is get busy with the logistics. You ring the right people, sort the paperwork, work out the dates, and you're genuinely useful to everyone in the room. A week later you're often somewhere else entirely, having booked a trip or thrown yourself into a new project, and you'll say you're fine and mean it. The feeling usually catches up in a quiet moment months on. The cost to the people around you is that they can't find you. Your partner wants to grieve alongside you and you've already moved to the next thing. What helps is staying put for a bit. Keep the same routine, see the same two friends, and let somebody sit with you before you plan anything.

You tend to fall for people through conversation, the long kind that goes late and wanders all over the place. Aquarius's opposite sign is Leo, and a lot of people with this Sun end up with someone warmer and more openly affectionate, someone who wants to hear that they're loved in so many words. The less obvious thing is that you show love by moving towards people, quite literally. You'll drive three hours to help with a flat, or change cities for a partner's job, and you assume that's understood as love. Often it isn't, and your partner is still waiting for you to say it. You also need someone who doesn't take your need for distance personally. A weekend alone, or a long walk after a row before you can talk, is how you come back, and a partner who follows you out the door usually makes it worse.

Mercury is messages and movement, and in Aquarius it likes systems, so you're good at work that gets people or information from one state to another. Relocation, logistics, IT migrations, change management, transport planning, immigration casework, helping people through redundancy, teaching adults who are retraining. You're often the one brought in when a team is in a mess, and you're good at getting them to the other side of it. The catch is that once things are calm you get restless. You like the crossing and you're a bit bored by the far shore, so you can end up changing jobs every three years without ever quite choosing to. That's fine if you know it about yourself. Talk it over with someone you trust before you hand in the next notice.

At twenty this slice of Aquarius often seems a little cooler than its friends, the one who talks everybody else through their breakups while keeping their own life tidy and fairly private. There's usually at least one big move early on, leaving home young, changing countries, dropping one course to start another. By the mid-thirties the pattern tends to catch up. Something you left without really feeling comes back, and you have to sit through it the slow way. That's often when people with this Sun get warmer, and a lot easier to be close to. The fifties tend to bring a settledness they didn't expect to want. A house they stay in, friends of thirty years, and a real knack for helping younger people through their own hard crossings.

The next time you've half made up your mind to leave something, a job, a flat, a friendship, a committee, tell one person while you're still deciding. Don't wait until the plan is finished. Say something like 'I'm thinking about going and I haven't worked it out yet.' It'll feel exposing, because you're used to arriving with the answer already sorted. But the people close to you get to come along for the crossing, and there's often a feeling or two in it you hadn't noticed.
